audience.programmeDescription: Students develop advanced French alongside work on French and Francophone literature, linguistics, cultural history and research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR combination studies literary form, life writing, literary theory and the circulation of texts across cultures, drawing on comparative history, visual culture and film. Leiden develops these practices in French through Francophone literature, period-specific seminars, linguistics and advanced written and spoken French.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC combines 60 EC of first-year study, 35 EC of later common courses, 30 EC of alternating courses taken once across years two and three, three 5-EC seminars, a 10-EC thesis and 30 EC of approved open choice. Two seminars must include research. The alternating courses run every other year; a resit does not provide a new teaching opportunity. Poetry and Theatre requires earlier French literature study and Written Expression; Metamorphoses of the Novel requires the earlier literature courses. Seminar entry requires at least 45 EC of first-year French study. Thesis entry requires the first-year examination, specified research preparation and written-expression requirements; thesis workshop participation is compulsory. Course choices and open space remain subject to university approval and overlap rules.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity.
Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status.
Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources.
Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline.
Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination.
Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory.
Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language.
Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes.
Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction.
Studies and develops creative communication through poetry, performance and critically articulated artistic practice.
Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings.
Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception.
This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present.
Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation.
Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization.
Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty.
Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation.
Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory.
Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation.
Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance.
Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks.
Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture.
Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production.
